Both commands bring changes from one branch into another. They differ in what they do to history.

Say you branched off `main`, and both branches have since gained commits:

```
      A---B---C   feature
     /
D---E---F---G     main
```

## Merge

```bash
git switch feature
git merge main
```

```
      A---B---C---M   feature
     /           /
D---E---F-------G     main
```

Git creates a **merge commit** `M` with two parents. Existing commits aren't changed. (If the branch you're merging into has no commits of its own, Git just moves its pointer forward by default. This is a "fast-forward", and it creates no merge commit.)

## Rebase

```bash
git switch feature
git rebase main
```

```
D---E---F---G              main
             \
              A'--B'--C'   feature
```

Git replays your commits on top of `main`. `A'`, `B'` and `C'` are **new commits** with new hashes, even if their changes are the same as the originals.

## Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| **History** | Shows when branches diverged and joined | Linear, as if you had started from the latest `main` |
| **Existing commits** | Preserved | Replaced |
| **Shared branches** | Safe | Disruptive unless everyone coordinates |
| **Conflicts** | Resolved once, for the combined result | Resolved commit by commit, so similar conflicts can recur |
| **Undo** | Reset or revert the merge (reverting has complications if you later re-merge) | Recover the old tip using `ORIG_HEAD` or the reflog |
| **Pushing afterward** | Normal push | Needs a force push if the old commits were already pushed |
| **Testing** | Old commits keep the context they were written and tested in | Replayed commits may never have been tested, and some may be broken even if the final one works |

## When to use each

**Rebase** when the commits are yours alone:
- Updating a local or personal feature branch before opening a pull request
- Cleaning up work-in-progress commits with `git rebase -i`, which lets you squash, reorder and reword them
- Avoiding unnecessary merge commits when pulling, with `git pull --rebase`

**Merge** when others depend on the history or you want to keep it:
- Updating a branch that several people are working on
- Bringing a finished feature into `main`, if you want a record of it as a unit (`--no-ff` forces a merge commit)
- Handling long-running branches such as release branches

## The main rule

**Don't rebase commits that others may have built on unless you've coordinated with them.** Their work still points to the old commits, which can lead to duplicate commits and confusing cleanup.

If you rebase a branch you've already pushed, use:

```bash
git push --force-with-lease
```

It refuses to push if the remote branch doesn't match what you expect, so it's safer than `--force`. A background fetch can weaken this protection by updating your expectation before you've looked at the new commits. Adding `--force-if-includes` helps guard against that.

## A gotcha during conflicts

"Ours" and "theirs" can seem reversed during a rebase. **"Ours" is the new base plus the commits replayed so far**, and **"theirs" is your commit being replayed**. To back out of a conflicted rebase, run `git rebase --abort`.

1. Rebase your own branch onto `main` to keep it current.
2. Merge it into `main` through a pull request.

Your team's convention matters more than which style is theoretically better, so follow it if there is one.

def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    if tags is None:

React compares props by reference (`Object.is`), not by contents, so an object created during render is a "new" prop every time:

```jsx
<Child config={{ size: 10 }} />  // new object on each parent render
```

Also, **by default a child re-renders whenever its parent renders, even if its props are identical.** To skip those renders, you need `React.memo` on the child and a stable reference for the object:

```jsx
const Child = React.memo(function Child({ config }) { /* ... */ });

function Parent() {
  const config = useMemo(() => ({ size }), [size]); // size: your prop or state
  return <Child config={config} />;
}
```

- **Constant object:** define it outside the component. You don't need `useMemo`.
- **Only a few fields needed:** pass primitives, such as `<Child size={size} />`.
- **Function or array props, including `children` JSX:** these also get new references each render. Use `useCallback` for functions and `useMemo` for arrays or JSX.
- **Still re-rendering:** the child's own state or a context it consumes may be changing, which `React.memo` doesn't block. The React DevTools Profiler can show why it rendered.
- **React Compiler:** if you have it enabled, it handles much of this memoization automatically.

The main pitfall is mutating an object and passing the same reference: a memoized child will then miss the update, so create a new object when the data changes. A re-render is also often cheap, so memoize when it causes a measurable problem. If you share your parent and child code, I can pinpoint the cause.
